steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the last years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods, and Machine Learning methods in particular, have been successful in real-life problems in a way that was unexpected only a few years ago. Many different areas contributed to this. Among them we can mention research on new theoretical algorithms, the increasing computational power of the latest generation of hardware, and the rapid access to huge amounts of data. All these factors together have led to the development of AI methods that are self-regulated and more and more complex.

Many of the AI models used today are based on backpropagation algorithms, which train and regulate themselves to reach a goal like classification, recommendation, or prediction. These self-regulating models get some kind of knowledge, since they successfully evaluate test data that is independent of the data used to train them. But this knowledge is usually expressed in a way that humans cannot read.

To fill the gap between the recent development of AI models and their use in society, many researchers have worked on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). XAI is a set of techniques that give clear, understandable, transparent, intelligible, trustworthy, and interpretable explanations of the decisions, predictions, and reasoning processes of AI models, instead of only showing their output. This is especially important in domains where AI decisions can have significant consequences on human life. A global taxonomy of interpretable AI, which aims to unify terminology so that regulations for developing ethical and reliable AI can be defined clearly and efficiently, is given in. A nice introduction and general vision can be found in. Another paper that clarifies definitions, concepts, and applications of XAI is.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the last years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods, and Machine Learning methods in particular, have been successful in real-life problems in a way that was unexpected only a few years ago. Many different areas contributed to this. Among them we can mention research on new theoretical algorithms, the increasing computational power of the latest generation of hardware, and the rapid access to huge amounts of data. All these factors together have led to the development of AI methods that are self-regulated and more and more complex.

Many of the AI models used today are based on backpropagation algorithms, which train and regulate themselves to reach a goal like classification, recommendation, or prediction. These self-regulating models get some kind of knowledge, since they successfully evaluate test data that is independent of the data used to train them. But this knowledge is usually expressed in a way that humans cannot read.

To fill the gap between the recent development of AI models and their use in society, many researchers have worked on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). XAI is a set of techniques that give clear, understandable, transparent, intelligible, trustworthy, and interpretable explanations of the decisions, predictions, and reasoning processes of AI models, instead of only showing their output. This is especially important in domains where AI decisions can have significant consequences on human life. A global taxonomy of interpretable AI, which aims to unify terminology so that regulations for developing ethical and reliable AI can be defined clearly and efficiently, is given in. A nice introduction and general vision can be found in. Another paper that clarifies definitions, concepts, and applications of XAI is.

Simplicial Map Neural Networks (SMNNs) were introduced in as a constructive approach to the problem of approximating a continuous function on a compact set in a triangulated space. Because the original goal of defining SMNNs was a constructive approach, their weights were not computed with an optimization process like usual neural networks, but with a deterministic calculus. Both the architecture of SMNNs and the computation of their weights are based on simplicial maps, which is a tool from combinatorial topology. SMNNs can also be used for classification and can be built to be robust to adversarial examples. Their architecture can also be reduced and still keep accuracy, and they are invariant to a transformation if the transformation preserves the barycentric coordinates (scale, rotation, symmetries, etc.). As they were defined in, SMNNs are two-hidden-layer feed-forward networks where the weights are precomputed from a triangulated convex polytope that surrounds the input data. Like other approximations of continuous functions with arbitrary precision (see, for example,), SMNNs have fixed weights. This means the weights only depend on the triangulation built with the points of the dataset as support set, and there is no training process.

So, some of the limitations of SMNNs up to now are that they are costly to compute, because the number of neurons is proportional to the number of simplices of the triangulation on the input dataset, and that they overfit and so do not generalize well. Because of this SMNNs have not been used in practice so far, even though relating simplicial maps to neural networks is a disruptive idea and builds a new bridge that can enrich both areas.

In this paper we propose a method that makes SMNNs efficient by reducing their size (the number of neurons, which depends on the vertices of the triangulation), and that makes SMNNs trainable and able to generalize. We also study how to select the vertices used to obtain the triangulation. SMNNs use the vertices of a simplex as part of the information needed for classification, but our approach is far from the classic instance-based methods of Machine Learning. Those methods are based on a deterministic computation using distances, while in our approach the weights are computed as the result of an optimization method in a space of probability distributions. Finally, from the XAI point of view, we will see that SMNNs are explainable models, since all the decision steps to compute their output are understandable and transparent, and so they are trustworthy.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall some concepts of computational topology and the definition of SMNNs. In Section 3 we develop some technical details that are needed for the SMNN training process, and the training process is introduced in Section 4. Section 5 is about the explainability of the model. Section 6 is about discussion and limitations. Finally the paper ends with some experiments and conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods in general and Machine Learning methods in particular have achieved success in real-life problems that was unexpected only a few years ago. Many different areas have contributed to this development, among them research on new theoretical algorithms, the increasing computational power of latest generation hardware, and rapid access to huge amounts of data. This combination of factors has led to the development of increasingly complex self-regulated AI methods.

Many AI models currently in use are based on backpropagation algorithms, which train and regulate themselves to achieve a goal such as classification, recommendation, or prediction. These self-regulating models achieve some kind of knowledge, as they successfully evaluate test data independent of the data used to train them. Nonetheless, this knowledge is usually expressed in a non-human-readable way.

To fill the gap between the recent development of AI models and their social use, many researchers have focused on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), a set of techniques that provide clear, understandable, transparent, intelligible, trustworthy, and interpretable explanations of the decisions, predictions, and reasoning processes of AI models, rather than just presenting their output, especially in domains where AI decisions can have significant consequences on human life. A global taxonomy of interpretable AI aimed at unifying terminology for clarity and efficiency in defining regulations for the development of ethical and reliable AI can be found in [1]. A nice introduction and general vision can be found in [2], and another clarifying paper with definitions, concepts, and applications of XAI is [3].

Simplicial Map Neural Networks (SMNNs) were introduced in [4] as a constructive approach to the problem of approximating a continuous function on a compact set in a triangulated space. Since the original aim was a constructive approach, the computation of their weights was not based on an optimization process, as usual in neural networks, but on a deterministic calculus. Both the architecture of SMNNs and the computation of their weights are based on a combinatorial topology tool called simplicial maps. SMNNs can be used for classification and can be constructed to be robust to adversarial examples [5]. Their architecture can also be reduced while maintaining accuracy [6], and they are invariant to a transformation if it preserves the barycentric coordinates (scale, rotation, symmetries, etc.). As defined in [4,6,5], SMNNs are two-hidden-layer feed-forward networks whose weights are precomputed from a triangulated convex polytope surrounding the input data. Like other approximations to continuous functions with arbitrary precision (see, for example, [7]), SMNNs have fixed weights: the weights depend only on the triangulation made with the points of the dataset as the support set, and no training process is applied.

In summary, some limitations of SMNNs so far are that they are costly to compute, since the number of neurons is proportional to the number of simplices of the triangulation supported on the input dataset, and that they suffer from overfitting and therefore do not generalize well. As a result, SMNNs have not been used in practice so far, although relating simplicial maps to neural networks is a disruptive idea that provides a new bridge able to enrich both areas.

In this paper, we propose a method that makes SMNNs efficient by reducing their size (in terms of the number of neurons, which depends on the vertices of the triangulation) and that makes SMNNs trainable and able to generalize. We also present a study of the selection of the vertices from which the triangulation is obtained. Although SMNNs consider the vertices of a simplex as part of the information needed for the classification task, our approach is far from classic Machine Learning instance-based methods. Those methods rely on a deterministic computation based on distances, whereas in our approach the weights are computed as the result of an optimization method in a probability distribution space. Finally, from an XAI point of view, we will see that SMNNs are explainable models, since all decision steps to compute their output are understandable and transparent, and therefore trustworthy.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls some concepts of computational topology and the definition of SMNNs. Section 3 develops several technical details needed for the SMNN training process, which is introduced in Section 4. Section 5 is devoted to the explainability of the model and Section 6 to discussion and limitations. The paper ends with some experiments and conclusions.

References:
[1] M. Graziani, L. Dutkiewicz, D. Calvaresi, A global taxonomy of interpretable ai: unifying the terminology for the technical and social sciences, Artif Intell Rev (2022). doi: 10.1007/s10462-022-10256-8 .
[2] C. Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning, 2 ed., Independently published, 2022. URL: https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book .
[3] W. J. Murdoch, C. Singh, K. Kumbier, et al, Definitions, methods, and applications in interpretable machine learning, PNAS (2019). URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1900654116 .
[4] E. Paluzo-Hidalgo, R. Gonzalez-Diaz, M. A. Gutiérrez-Naranjo, Two-hidden-layer feed-forward networks are universal approximators: A constructive approach, Neural Netw 131 (2020) 29–36. doi: 10.1016/j.neunet.2020.07.021 .
[5] E. Paluzo-Hidalgo, R. Gonzalez-Diaz, M. A. Gutiérrez-Naranjo, J. Heras, Simplicial-map neural networks robust to adversarial examples, Mathematics 9 (2021a) 169. doi: 10.3390/math9020169 .
